title: Does Mr. Olympia know how to train BACK? (Analyzing Chris Bumstead's Workout w/ Will Tennyson)
summary: NH analyses a Chris Bumstead back workout filmed with Will Tennyson to show why an enhanced pro's bro-split back day (15-20 sets, drop sets, no hip hinge) is wrong for naturals. He explains the baseline concept of intensity, junk volume, rep quality and exercise order, and recommends 1-2 back exercises per session, opening with a heavy hip hinge or pull, and adding volume through frequency instead.
claims: Teenagers copy their idols' workouts without thinking; copying an enhanced pro is the worst mistake a natural can make
The bro split (one muscle per day) is the worst way for naturals to train: too low frequency and too much volume per session; enhanced lifters can recover from it
The upper back is the one muscle group where a bro-split style day makes most sense because it has huge work capacity, but even then mostly for advanced naturals with built foundations
Bumstead and Tennyson did about 6 exercises and 15-20 sets for back, mostly with drop sets; spread those sets across the week instead
Rep quality degrades through a session as fatigue builds; past a point extra sets just add fatigue that naturals cannot convert into stimulus
10 hard back sets once a week lose to 4 sets three times a week (12 sets, better recovery, higher intensity); repeating 10 sets 3x/week would give 30
The fewer sets you do in a session, the more intense each can be; for most people the sweet spot is 2 exercises per muscle (1 for novices, 3 for some advanced) before moving on
Baseline concept: you start a session at 100% capacity and dig into it with each set; when a weight under 50% of your max feels hard you are doing junk volume
Distinguish absolute intensity (what you can lift fresh) from relative intensity late in a session; a huge drop, e.g. rowing 3 plates down to 1, means the later reps were irrelevant
Being destroyed after a workout is not a goal; it hurts frequency and the ability to return to the gym
Always open a back day with a heavy hip hinge or heavy pull (e.g. heavy row from the floor or heavy pull-up variation), never a light pulldown or machine, since you are freshest at the start
Bro splits separate back and legs, so back days lack synergistic posterior chain work and leg days cram too many exercises into one weekly session
Heavy hip hinges build back thickness because the upper back works isometrically to stabilise the load, and they can replace one or two back exercises
Bumstead does high-rep heavy deadlifts that have a terrible stimulus-to-fatigue ratio; he can handle it, you cannot
The back works as a whole; doing 4 horizontal pulls and 1 vertical pull fatigues all of it, so rear delt work placed later is limited by a tired back
If you find yourself pacing sets to survive later exercises, the program is poorly built
More is not always better; enough is better, just enough to grow
Traps often fail to grow because trap exercises are placed at the end of the session when fatigued; order dictates development
Bumstead may wing his workouts thanks to instinct and PEDs; naturals should write a plan and prioritise lagging muscles by placing them first
For naturals: 1-2 back pulls per session (one vertical, one horizontal), e.g. 4 sets each, then build volume over time
Start with low volume and high quality reps, then expand; starting with too much volume forces you to shrink back later
You should leave the gym with some energy left, wanting to come back; being wiped out every session means working dumb, not hard
Tennyson probably needed 7-10 days to recover from that back session while Bumstead was fine
Drop sets on every set are a bad idea for naturals: dropping to a third of your working weight and still struggling is junk volume chased for sensation and pump
Being out of breath during lifting means you prioritise cardiovascular over muscular endurance; fix your cardio or your methods
If a session cannot be repeated within about 5 days because recovery is insufficient, it is a bad session; good sessions are repeatable for years
Back guidelines: never more than 3 exercises or about 10 sets per day; add volume via frequency, e.g. vertical pulls Monday, horizontal Wednesday, pulldown variation Friday
You can train back every session if fatigue is managed, as in his train-back-every-day program
Tennyson's normal approach of one row and one pulldown (about 8 sets) then repeating two days later is the better natural method
exercises: open the back day with it
back thickness and posterior chain frequency; can replace 1-2 back exercises
Light lat pulldown or machine row
